To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pigs fed a diet contaminated with 385 microg of AFB1 per kg for 4 weeks had low EROD activity but no other changes in liver P450 activity.
subchronic exposure of pigs to aflatoxin (AF) B1 resulted in the selective impairment of cytochrome P-450 (P450) 1A and 3A enzymes.
the liver of the pig exposed to aflatoxin is a good model to study the mechanism of action of this mycotoxin.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of aflatoxin on the cytochrome P-450 enzymes in the pig liver.
the effects of aflatoxin B(1) (AFB(1)) on the expression of cytochrome P(450) enzymes in the pig liver.
a better understanding of the effects of aflatoxin B(1) (AFB(1)) exposure on the expression of liver drug-metabolising enzymes in pigs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

P450 1 and 3 enzymes are more sensitive to AFB1 toxicity in pig than P450 2 enzymes and that the lowest dose (385 microg A FB1/kg of feed) is sufficient to induce a specific inhibition of EROD and testosterone 6 beta-hydroxylation activities.
P450 1 and P450 2 are the major targets of AFB(1), while P450 3 appears to be more specifically affected by this mycotoxin.
AFB1 is an inhibitor of P450 1 and P450 2A and a substrate for P450 3C, P450 3E and P450 4A.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
pigs fed 867 microg of AFB1/kg feed for 28 days developed mild degenerative hepatoxicity without clinical symptoms and with a significant alteration in the expression of P450 1 and 3A enzymes.
the pig is an appropriate animal model for studying the effects of AFB1 on P450 1 and P450 2 enzymes.
the effects on P450 enzymes are dose-related and the most important effects were observed in the animals with the highest AFB1 exposure.
The main takeaway from our work is that
pigs are more sensitive to the hepatocarcinogenic effects of AFB1 than rats, and that this difference is due to the higher levels of aflatoxin-DNA adducts found in pig liver.
pigs are a good model to study the effects of dietary AFB1 on the liver and its biotransformation enzymes.
AFB1 can affect liver biotransformation enzymes in pigs even at doses that did not cause clinical sign of liver damage.
